headline: NZ MPs Advance Credit-Law Changes as Social Housing Rent Rises Draw Fire
summary: Parliament debated pressure on household budgets, including proposed increases to social housing rents and changes to consumer-credit protections, while the Government defended its approach as fairer and more efficient. Opposition MPs also pressed Prime Minister Christopher Luxon over missing records relating to a briefing note involving Fonterra and Z Energy, and ministers announced new energy and conservation initiatives. Several bills and a regulatory notice advanced, amid sharp disagreement over consumer protections, public-sector oversight and the Government’s relationship with business.

topicSummaries.topic: Social Housing Rent Changes Face Cost-of-Living Challenge
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Higher social housing contributions could leave some tenants, including pensioners and people with disabilities, with less money for essentials such as food, heating and transport.
topicSummaries.content: Labour and Green MPs challenged the Government’s planned social housing changes, citing an average rent increase of $31 a week and asking how tenants on fixed or limited incomes would manage. Housing Minister Chris Bishop said the changes aim to make support fairer between people in similar circumstances and better target social housing to those with persistent needs. He said roughly 30 percent of people receiving social housing assistance earn enough to manage a lower-quartile private rental, while about 19,000 families or applicants are on the social housing register. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon defended the reforms, saying they are intended to improve fairness and help some people move towards independence.

keyExchanges.speaker: Kieran McAnulty (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: How does he expect a pensioner in social housing to cover the average $31 a week increase in rent when this outstrips the recent annual increase to New Zealand super of $16 a week?

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Bishop (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The Government is making changes to the social housing contribution that people make in order to improve the equity of the entire system.

topicSummaries.topic: Credit Bill Advances Amid Dispute Over Consumer Rights and Bank Litigation
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Changes to credit rules and oversight could affect borrowers’ protections, access to credit and ability to seek remedies when lenders have breached requirements.
topicSummaries.content: The Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Amendment Bill was reported back to the House with amendments after its committee stage, with government changes passing 67 votes to 55. The bill shifts consumer-credit oversight from the Commerce Commission to the Financial Markets Authority (FMA), with the transfer due to take effect on 1 July 2026. Labour argued the bill weakens safeguards, including protections for people using buy-now-pay-later services, and said provisions could prevent some consumers from bringing claims against banks if those claims had not already been filed. Commerce and Consumer Affairs Minister Cameron Brewer said existing buy-now-pay-later rules would remain under close monitoring and that the FMA would have the tools to oversee lenders. The bill’s final passage was not recorded in the proceedings provided.

keyExchanges.speaker: Arena Williams (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: The particular criticism is that the affordability exemption under the September 2024 regulation means that “buy now, pay later” providers can choose to be exempt from the obligation to undertake affordability assessments.

keyExchanges.speaker: Cameron Brewer (National)
keyExchanges.quote: “Buy now, pay later” is regulated. It is under watch, and it will continue to be under a close watch thanks to MBIE, and it will also soon be thanks to the FMA.

topicSummaries.topic: Luxon Says His Office Has No Record of 2024 Fonterra-Z Energy Contact
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The dispute raises questions about record-keeping and how corporate proposals may be considered when the Government is making decisions that affect climate policy and court proceedings.
topicSummaries.content: Labour leader Chris Hipkins questioned Luxon about a 2024 briefing note prepared on behalf of defendants in the Smith v Fonterra case that proposed legislation to halt the litigation. Luxon said he understood that someone who had since left his office received the note, but his office had no record or recollection of related meetings or whether the proposal was passed to other officials. He said his office had asked Ministerial Services to remind staff of their record-keeping obligations. Luxon defended the Government’s position that the State, rather than courts or businesses, should set the climate framework. The Speaker accepted Chlöe Swarbrick’s request for an urgent debate on the handling of Official Information Act documents, but that debate is not included in the proceedings provided.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Hipkins (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Was Z Energy and Fonterra’s proposed amendment to New Zealand’s climate change laws passed on by anyone in his office to any other Minister, their staff, or any Government officials; if so, who?

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Well, as I’ve said to the member, there is no record or recollection of that interaction in 2024. Ideally, there should have been a record kept; there wasn’t.

topicSummaries.topic: Gas Transition Loan Scheme Could Back Up to $1.2B in Business Loans
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The scheme is intended to help large gas users switch energy sources and reduce the risk of supply shortages affecting industrial operations and jobs.
topicSummaries.content: Energy Minister Simeon Brown said Budget 2026 provides for a Gas Transition Loan Guarantee Scheme for businesses using more than 1,000 gigajoules of reticulated gas a year. Eligible businesses could borrow to cut gas use by at least 15 percent, with the Crown guaranteeing 80 percent of each loan; individual loans would be capped at $50 million and up to $1.2 billion could be written. Brown said known remaining gas reserves were 23 percent lower than a year earlier and argued the scheme would support jobs and energy resilience. Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick questioned why the Government had scrapped an earlier gas transition plan and challenged its support for new fossil-fuel production. Brown defended the scheme as a way to help businesses transition while encouraging domestic supply.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chlöe Swarbrick (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: If the Minister is so concerned about “picking winners”, what then does he make of the Government’s decision to provide a $200 million taxpayer subsidy for the production of new fossil fuels?

keyExchanges.speaker: Simeon Brown (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Well, it’s about co-investing to ensure we actually get indigenous gas out of the ground.

topicSummaries.topic: Government Defends Public-Service Cuts Amid Front-Line Job Concerns
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Changes to staffing could affect the availability of services people rely on, including border security, food safety, child protection and emergency management.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Camilla Belich asked whether the Government could rule out cutting specific front-line roles as part of its public-service overhaul. Public Service Minister Paul Goldsmith did not give that assurance, saying the Government was focused on reducing duplication and administration so more resources could support front-line services. He said core public-service staffing had risen from 47,000 in 2017 to 65,000 after the current Government took office and argued that level was unsustainable. Finance Minister Nicola Willis separately defended public-service reductions, saying service improvements in areas such as elective surgery and education showed staffing numbers did not automatically determine outcomes.

keyExchanges.speaker: Camilla Belich (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Can he rule out disestablishing the roles of social workers responsible for protecting our vulnerable children; if not, why not?

keyExchanges.speaker: Paul Goldsmith (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The broad point that I would make around the public services is that the more efficient we can be with back-office delivery of functions such as finance and human resources and information technology—all those things—the more opportunities we have to invest in front-line services where they are required.

topicSummaries.topic: House Approves First Exclusions Under Regulatory Standards Act
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The notice sets which types of legislation will be exempt from a new regulatory assessment framework, shaping how laws affecting public services and everyday life are scrutinised.
topicSummaries.content: The House approved the first notice under the Regulatory Standards Act 2025, excluding specified categories of legislation from the Act’s requirements. The categories include emergency powers, international agreements, constitutional matters, Crown agreements with iwi and hapū, and administrative instruments. Labour and the Greens supported the notice while raising concerns about overlap between the new executive-led framework and Parliament’s existing scrutiny role; Te Pāti Māori also supported the exclusions but said the Act itself should be repealed. Regulation Minister David Seymour said the framework would promote transparent, high-quality lawmaking. The Regulations Review Committee recommended approval by consensus, while members raised questions about the criteria used for some exclusions.

keyExchanges.speaker: David Seymour (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: If a law or regulation is going to impact on a person’s rights or property, then we should ensure that it is as clear and transparent as possible to the people what those impacts are.

keyExchanges.speaker: Arena Williams (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: The committee’s position was this: that parliamentary scrutiny of secondary legislation belongs to the House and its committees, not to executive-created bodies.

topicSummaries.topic: $79M Boost Announced for Wilding Pine Control
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The funding is intended to protect farmland, native habitats and water catchments, with potential flow-on effects for electricity supplies and power costs.
topicSummaries.content: The Government announced an additional $79 million over three years for controlling wilding pines, taking total funding to $109 million. Conservation Minister Tama Potaka said $30 million would come from the international visitor levy, while Biosecurity Minister Andrew Hoggard said the funding would support control work on public and private land. Hoggard said more than two million hectares were affected and that dense infestations could reduce river flows in key catchments. He also said Biosecurity New Zealand would adapt the existing control plan into a national pest management plan to support longer-term funding and consistent rules.

keyExchanges.speaker: Andrew Hoggard (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Controlling wildings isn’t just about the view; it’s keeping water in the lakes, and pressure off our power bills.

keyExchanges.speaker: Tama Potaka (National)
keyExchanges.quote: As part of the $79 million uplift for wilding control the Government announced on Sunday, we’ve committed $30 million of funding from the international visitor levy, the IVL, to wilding control over the next three years.

topicSummaries.topic: New Stalking Offence Takes Effect With Penalty of up to Five Years
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: People affected by repeated stalking and harassment now have a specific criminal offence that can carry a prison sentence.
topicSummaries.content: Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith told the House that the Crimes Legislation (Stalking and Harassment) Amendment Act had commenced. The new offence applies where a person carries out a pattern of specified behaviour that they know is likely to cause fear or distress; the pattern is defined as two specified acts within a two-year period. The maximum penalty is five years’ imprisonment. Goldsmith said the law followed calls for stronger action and was intended to put victims at the centre of the justice system.

keyExchanges.speaker: Paul Goldsmith (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Stalking is now a criminal offence punishable by up to five years’ imprisonment.

keyExchanges.speaker: Rima Nakhle (National)
keyExchanges.quote: What does the Crimes Legislation (Stalking and Harassment) Amendment Act do to protect New Zealanders from stalking?

conclusion: The day’s proceedings advanced government reforms, but left unresolved how far efficiency and market flexibility should go when they may affect household costs, consumer rights and public accountability.
